analysis.one_liner: Makes two years of community college tuition-free and covers college costs for students who commit to public service.
analysis.headline: A Democratic senator introduced the bill in May 2018 with no cosponsors, and it never received a committee hearing or a vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create three big programs. First, the federal government would send states and Indian Tribes grants to waive community college tuition and fees for eligible students, with states picking up 25% of the cost and federal funding rising to about $15.7 billion a year. Second, historically Black colleges and other minority-serving institutions would get grants to cut or waive tuition for low-income students. Third, students who commit to at least three years of work in a public service job after graduating could get their undergraduate cost of attendance paid, and existing federal loan borrowers in public service jobs would get portions of their loans canceled over each two-year stretch of service, adding up to full cancellation after ten years.
analysis.who_benefits: Community college students, low-income students, and students who commit to public service careers — including teachers, nurses, law enforcement, and government workers. States and Tribes would also receive federal funds, and community colleges and minority-serving institutions would gain enrollment and revenue as tuition dropped.

how_it_helps.text: The federal government would grant states and Indian Tribes funds to waive community college resident tuition and fees for eligible students, with the federal share covering up to 75% of average tuition and fees and the state share 25% [S3].

Historically Black colleges and universities and other minority-serving institutions with at least 35% low-income enrollment would receive grants to waive or significantly reduce tuition and fees for their students [S3].

Students who have finished an associate degree or 60 credits and commit to at least three years of public service work after graduation would have the cost of tuition, fees, and on-campus room and board paid through a new grant program at public and private nonprofit four-year colleges [S3].

Federal Direct Loan borrowers in public service jobs would have 15% of their loan canceled after 2 years, another 15% after 4, 20% after 6, 20% after 8, and the final 30% after 10 years — full cancellation after a decade of service [S3].

The bill appropriates specific federal sums for the community college program, starting at about $1.5 billion and rising to about $15.7 billion per year by 2027, plus separate funding for the minority-serving institution grants [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through new mandatory appropriations growing into the tens of billions per year, and states, which would have to cover 25% of community college tuition costs and maintain their higher-education funding. Students who fail the program's terms — a 3.0 GPA or the three-year service commitment — would have their grants converted into loans with interest.

drawbacks.text: The community college program alone would grow to roughly $15.7 billion per year in federal appropriations by 2027, with separate funding on top for minority-serving institutions and the public service grant program, a major new ongoing federal expense [S3].

States must cover 25% of the community college tuition cost and keep their higher-education funding from falling below prior levels, which some states could not absorb without cutting other programs [S3].

The public service grant carries strict terms: students must maintain a 3.0 GPA and finish in two years, and if they drop out or refuse the three-year service commitment, their grants convert to a loan with interest accruing from the date of the award [S3].

The aid is narrower than universal help: community college funding is limited to transferable academic programs or in-demand occupational credentials, eligibility lapses after three years of benefits, and the loan forgiveness applies only to public service workers, not all borrowers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would put real money in the hands of low-income and working-class students: two tuition-free community college years, reduced-cost degrees at minority-serving institutions, and debt-free college in exchange for public service, plus faster loan forgiveness for existing public servants. The cost is large and permanent — federal spending that grows past $17 billion a year — and the public service grant's repayment penalty, which converts aid into an interest-bearing loan for students who stumble, is harsher than typical grant rules. The state match and maintenance-of-effort requirements also shift real costs to states. On balance, the benefits flow overwhelmingly to ordinary students and the costs are broadly distributed through taxes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health and education committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill in the Senate on May 24, 2018 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced; that was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained anything new: community college students kept paying tuition, public service borrowers kept the slower existing forgiveness system, and no new federal spending was created. The status quo — higher tuition costs for students and no federal tuition waiver — continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply expired untouched

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 24, 2018 and delivered introductory remarks, but attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on May 24, 2018, allowing it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no Republican or other Democrats cosponsored, so the bill died with support demonstrated only from its single Democratic sponsor [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would make community colleges tuition-free for eligible students, funneling federal and state money to them and likely increasing enrollment. Students and colleges would both gain.

industries.industry: Historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: New grants would pay a per-student rebate to waive or cut tuition for low-income students, boosting institutional revenue and affordability at the same time.

industries.industry: Public and private nonprofit four-year colleges
industries.note: They would receive federal funding to cover cost of attendance for public-service-bound transfer students, though private nonprofits would have to match the federal grant for middle-income students.

The bill funds only public and nonprofit institutions, so for-profit colleges would gain no new students or dollars from these programs and would lose some prospective enrollees to the cheaper public alternative.

Accelerated forgiveness would cancel more loan principal for public service borrowers, reducing outstanding debt, though the Direct Loan program is run by the Education Department rather than a private industry.
